facts.value: Three types of workplace violence: physical violence (hitting, kicking, beating, punching, biting, and using objects); psychological violence (threats or coercion); sexual violence (attempted/completed non-consensual sex act).
Interpersonal violence is committed by workers or patients and their families, primarily manifesting as verbal abuse.

Organizational coercion may include excessive workloads, mandatory shifts, involuntary placement in another part of the workplace, low salaries, denial of benefits/overtime, and poor working environment.
Factors can be divided into environmental, organizational, and individual psychosocial factors.
Environmental factors include the specific setting, long patient wait times, frequent interruptions, uncertainty regarding patients' treatment, and heavy workloads.
Organizational factors include inefficient teamwork, organizational injustice, lack of aggression- and stress-management programs, and distrust between colleagues.
Individual psychosocial factors may include young and inexperienced nurses, previous experiences with violence, and lack of communication skills.
Misunderstandings may occur due to the communication barrier between nurses and patients.
80% of serious violent incidents in health care centers were committed by patients.
Workplace violence has negative emotional and physical impacts on nurses, causing feelings of depersonalization, dehumanization, exhaustion, and stress.
Nurses have reported burn-out due to frequent exposure to workplace violence.
Nursing is a professional health care occupation.
RNs treat patients, record their medical history, provide emotional support, and provide follow-up care.
Nurses may act as assistants to doctors in some capacities, such as in the emergency department or in trauma care.
Options in hospital settings include pediatrics, neonatal, maternity, OBGYN, geriatrics, orthopedics, medical-surgical, operating room, ambulatory, and nurse anesthetists and informatics.
Other options include community health, mental health, clinical nursing specialists, and nurse midwives.
Nurses in Canada practice in a wide variety of settings, with various levels of training and experience. They provide evidence-based care and educate their patients about health and disease.
Seven National Historic Sites of Canada related to nursing have been designated.

Five nurses' residences were designated in commemoration of the growing professionalism of nursing: the Ann Baillie Building, Begbie Hall, Hersey Pavilion, Pavillon Mailloux, and the St. Boniface Hospital Nurses' Residence.
La Corne Nursing Station and the Wilberforce Red Cross Outpost were designated in part to honor the role played by nurses in delivering health care to isolated areas.
Every nurse registered in the General or Extended class is required under the Registered Health Professions Act, 1991, to participate in the Quality Assurance (QA) program.
Nurses demonstrate their commitment to continually improving their practice by annually engaging in a written reflection, an analysis of the year, and setting two learning goals.
